ABSTRACT
Emotion detection from text is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that enables systems to identify and classify the emotional state conveyed by written language. This project presents an Emotion Detection System trained on a large-scale multi-class dataset comprising 106,355 text samples spanning eleven distinct emotion categories: anger, empty, enthusiasm, fun, happiness, hate, love, neutral, relief, sadness, and surprise.
The system employs a classical machine learning pipeline in which raw text is preprocessed through lowercasing, punctuation removal, stop-word filtering, and lemmatization using NLTK. Feature extraction is performed using TF-IDF vectorization with trigram support (n-gram range 1–3) and sublinear term-frequency scaling across a vocabulary of up to 10,000 features. Two classification algorithms are trained and evaluated: Logistic Regression with grid-searched regularization and LinearSVC, both configured with class-weight balancing to address class imbalance.
Model selection is performed via 3-fold cross-validated GridSearchCV, and both models are benchmarked on a held-out 20% test split using accuracy, per-class precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices. The system concludes with an interactive prediction loop allowing real-time inference: Logistic Regression outputs top-3 emotion probabilities while SVM provides a hard-label prediction.
The proposed system demonstrates that well-tuned classical ML pipelines can achieve competitive emotion classification performance, offering interpretability and computational efficiency compared to deep learning approaches.
1. INTRODUCTION
Emotion detection from text is the task of automatically identifying the emotional tone expressed in written language. As digital communication proliferates across social media, messaging platforms, and online communities, the ability to automatically infer human emotions from text has become increasingly valuable in applications ranging from customer sentiment analysis to mental health monitoring, chatbot development, and human–computer interaction.
1.1 Motivation
Manual emotion labelling is time-consuming and subjective. An automated system that can reliably classify text into fine-grained emotion categories enables large-scale analysis of user sentiment, early detection of distress in mental-health contexts, and improved personalisation in conversational agents. The availability of large, labelled datasets makes supervised machine learning an attractive and effective approach for this task.
